finalText:
For an external classic script, both `async` and `defer` let the browser download the script while it keeps parsing the HTML. The difference is when the script runs. A `defer` script waits until parsing has finished and runs before `DOMContentLoaded`, and several `defer` scripts run in the order they appear in the document. An `async` script runs as soon as it has downloaded, in no guaranteed order, and its timing relative to `DOMContentLoaded` is not fixed. Neither attribute does anything on an inline classic script. Module scripts are deferred by default, so `defer` does nothing on them, while `async` works on both external and inline modules.

## 1. A plain classic script (`<script src>` with neither attribute)
With neither attribute, "the script is fetched and evaluated immediately, blocking parsing until these are both complete" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html). MDN says the same: such a script "blocks parsing, not rendering" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script).

## 2. `defer` (external classic scripts)
- **Parsing:** the script "will be fetched in parallel and evaluated when the page has finished parsing" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html). The spec adds each deferred script to the document's "list of scripts that will execute when the document has finished parsing", and the parser runs them itself (same URL).
- **`DOMContentLoaded`:** the script runs "after the document has been parsed, but before firing DOMContentLoaded event". A deferred script also holds back `DOMContentLoaded` until it "has loaded and finished evaluating" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script). MDN's event page agrees: the event fires once parsing is done and all deferred scripts have downloaded and run (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/DOMContentLoaded_event).
- **Order:** "Scripts with the defer attribute will execute in the order in which they appear in the document" (MDN, same URL). web.dev says the same (https://web.dev/articles/efficiently-load-third-party-javascript). Because the spec uses a *list* for deferred scripts, document order is kept.

## 3. `async` (external classic scripts)
- **Parsing:** the script is "fetched in parallel to parsing and evaluated as soon as it is available (potentially before parsing completes)" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html). So the download doesn't block the parser, but running the script can. web.dev notes that async scripts "can interrupt DOM building if they finish downloading while the parser is still at work" (https://web.dev/articles/efficiently-load-third-party-javascript).
- **Order:** none is guaranteed. The spec puts async scripts in a "set of scripts that will execute as soon as possible", which is a *set*, not an ordered list, and each one runs when it is ready (spec URL above). web.dev says async scripts are likely to run out of document order.
- **`DOMContentLoaded`:** the event "doesn't wait for … async scripts" (MDN event page). An async script can run before the event, if it is ready while parsing is still going on, or after it. MDN itself lists `<script async>` as a case where your code may run after `DOMContentLoaded` has already fired.
- **Both attributes set:** `async` wins. Adding `defer` only gives older browsers that support `defer` but not `async` a fallback (spec). MDN says the element "will act as if only the async attribute is specified".

## 4. Inline classic scripts
In the spec's attribute table, `async` and `defer` are not allowed on inline classic scripts. The async/defer handling only applies when the type is "classic" and the element has a `src`, or when the type is "module". Any other script is executed immediately, unless a style sheet that blocks scripts makes it wait (spec URL). MDN warns that using either attribute without `src` "would have no effect". web.dev adds that inline scripts "block the parser until the script is parsed and executed" (https://web.dev/learn/performance/optimize-resource-loading).

## 5. `type="module"`
Modules are deferred by default. Without `async`, a module and its dependencies are fetched while parsing continues and run when parsing has finished, and "The defer attribute has no effect on module scripts" (spec). They go in the same ordered "finished parsing" list as `defer` scripts, so they also run before `DOMContentLoaded` (MDN event page). With `async`, "the module script and all its dependencies will be fetched in parallel to parsing, and the module script will be evaluated as soon as it is available". Unlike classic scripts, `async` is allowed on *inline* module scripts as well (spec table). web.dev also says inline module scripts are deferred automatically.

## Where the sources disagree
- **Async and `DOMContentLoaded`.** A note on MDN's event page says `DOMContentLoaded` "is fired after the execution of these scripts, but before the execution of scripts with async". The spec says async scripts run "potentially before parsing completes", and web.dev agrees they can interrupt parsing. Both mean an async script can run *before* `DOMContentLoaded`. The same MDN page elsewhere says only that the event doesn't wait for async scripts. I'd go with the spec: there is no fixed order between async scripts and `DOMContentLoaded`.
- **"Same time" or "before".** web.dev's resource-loading page says deferred scripts run when parsing finishes, which "occurs at the same time as the browser's DOMContentLoaded event". MDN and the other web.dev article are more precise: deferred scripts run *before* the event, and the event waits for them.
- **What I couldn't fetch.** The spec's parsing chapter ("The end"), which spells out the steps for running deferred scripts and then firing `DOMContentLoaded`, returned 404 at https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html. The "before `DOMContentLoaded`" claim therefore rests on MDN and web.dev, plus the scripting chapter's description of the parser-run list.
